paragraphs: Unfortunately for the good sense of mankind, their fallibility carries far less weight in practice than in theory. Everyone knows that he can be wrong, yet few think it necessary to take precautions against their own fallibility. Few admit that an opinion they feel very certain of may be one of the errors to which they confess they are liable. Absolute princes, and others accustomed to unlimited deference, usually feel complete confidence in their opinions on nearly every subject. People more happily placed sometimes hear their views disputed and are sometimes corrected. Even they place unbounded reliance on the opinions shared by those around them. The less a man trusts his own solitary judgment, the more he relies on the infallibility of "the world" in general.

For each individual, the world means the part of it he comes into contact with: his party, his sect, his church, his class of society. A man for whom it means his whole country or his own age may be called almost liberal by comparison. Nor is his faith in this collective authority shaken by knowing that other ages, countries, churches and parties have thought the exact reverse. He leaves it to his own world to be right against the dissenting worlds of others. It never troubles him that mere accident decided which world he relies on. The same causes that make him a Churchman in London would have made him a Buddhist or a Confucian in Pekin. Yet it is evident that ages are no more infallible than individuals. Every age has held many opinions that later ages judged not only false but absurd. Many opinions now general will surely be rejected in the future.

The objection to this argument would probably run as follows. Forbidding the spread of error involves no greater assumption of infallibility than anything else public authority does on its own judgment. Judgment is given to men so that they may use it. Should they be told not to use it at all because it may be used wrongly? To prohibit what they think harmful is not to claim freedom from error. It is to fulfil their duty of acting on their conscientious conviction, although they are fallible. If we never acted on our opinions because they might be wrong, we would neglect all our interests and duties. An objection that applies to all conduct cannot be a valid objection to any conduct in particular.

Governments and individuals, such reasoners say, must form the truest opinions they can and never impose them unless quite sure. But once sure, it is cowardice to let dangerous doctrines spread without restraint because less enlightened times persecuted opinions now believed true. Governments have also made mistakes in other matters, laying on bad taxes and making unjust wars. Ought we therefore to have no taxes and no wars? Men and governments must act to the best of their ability. There is no absolute certainty, but there is assurance sufficient for the purposes of human life. We must assume our opinion to be true to guide our own conduct. So, they conclude, we assume no more when we forbid bad men to pervert society with opinions we regard as false and pernicious.
